l: city (Samaria), The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 7
s: The city is suffering famine, which leads the lepers to reject entering it. The king fears the Syrians are waiting to take its people alive and get in, but the report proves true that they have fled, and the people go out to plunder.

l: camp of the Syrians, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 7
s: The camp is found abandoned at twilight, with horses and donkeys tied and the tents as they were. The lepers take goods from two tents, and the people of the city later plunder it.

l: people (of Samaria), The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 7
s: The people go out and plunder the camp of the Syrians, so a seah of fine flour sells for a shekel and two measures of barley for a shekel, according to the Lord's word. In the gate they trample the captain, who dies.

l: The Second Book of Kings, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 8
s: Elisha warns the woman whose son he restored to flee a seven-year famine, and on her return the king, while hearing Gehazi recount Elisha's deeds, orders her house and land restored. Elisha then goes to Damascus, where the sick Benhadad sends Hazael to ask whether he will recover; Elisha says Benhadad will die and that Hazael will be king and bring terrible violence on Israel. Hazael tells Benhadad he will recover, then smothers him with a wet cloth and reigns. The chapter also records the evil reign of Jehoram of Judah, marked by Edom's revolt, and the one-year evil reign of his son Ahaziah, who joins Joram of Israel against Hazael and visits the wounded Joram at Jezreel.

l: Elisha, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 8
s: Elisha warns the woman to leave for seven years because of a famine called by the LORD. In Damascus he tells Hazael that Benhadad will surely die, stares at him until he is ashamed, weeps, and foretells the violence Hazael will do to Israel and that Hazael will be king over Syria.

l: Shunammite woman, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 8
s: The woman obeys Elisha's word and lives in the land of the Philistines for seven years. On returning she begs the king for her house and land, and the king appoints an officer to restore all that was hers along with the produce of the fields since she left.

l: Gehazi, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 8
s: Gehazi is talking with the king, telling him of Elisha's great deeds, including restoring the dead to life. When the woman appears, he identifies her and her son to the king as the ones Elisha restored to life.

l: king (king who spoke with Gehazi), The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 8
s: The king asks Gehazi to tell him all the great things Elisha has done. When the woman begs for her house and land, he questions her and appoints an officer to restore all that was hers and the fruits of the field since she left.

l: Hazael, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 8
s: Hazael is sent by Benhadad with forty camels' burden of gifts to ask Elisha whether the king will recover. Told by Elisha that he will be king and do great evil to Israel, he tells Benhadad he will recover, then the next day smothers him with a wet cloth and reigns in his place. He later fights Joram and Ahaziah at Ramoth Gilead.

l: Benhadad, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 8
s: Benhadad, king of Syria, is sick and sends Hazael to inquire of the LORD through Elisha. Elisha says he will surely die, and Hazael kills him the next day with a thick wet cloth spread over his face.

l: LORD, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 8
s: The LORD calls for a seven-year famine and shows Elisha that Benhadad will die and that Hazael will be king over Syria. He refuses to destroy Judah for the sake of his servant David, to whom he promised a lamp for his children always.

l: Joram, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 8
s: Joram, king of Israel, is wounded by the Syrians in the war against Hazael at Ramoth Gilead (at Ramah). He returns to Jezreel to be healed, where Ahaziah comes to see him.

l: Jehoram, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 8
s: Jehoram (also called Joram), son of Jehoshaphat, begins to reign over Judah in the fifth year of Joram of Israel, at age thirty-two, and reigns eight years. He walks in the way of Israel's kings and Ahab's house, having married Ahab's daughter, and does evil. He strikes the Edomites at Zair by night but cannot end their revolt, and he is buried in David's city with Ahaziah succeeding him.

l: Judah, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 8
s: Judah is ruled by Jehoram and then Ahaziah, both of whom do evil, yet the LORD will not destroy it for David's sake. In Jehoram's days Edom and Libnah revolt from its control.

l: Edom, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 8
s: Edom revolts from Judah's rule in Jehoram's days and sets up its own king. Jehoram strikes the Edomites at Zair, but they flee to their tents and Edom stays free of Judah to this day.

l: Edomite revolt, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 8
s: In Jehoram's reign Edom breaks away from Judah and makes a king over itself. Jehoram crosses to Zair and strikes the Edomites who surround him, but the revolt endures to this day, and Libnah revolts at the same time.

l: Ahaziah, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 8
s: Ahaziah, son of Jehoram and Athaliah, becomes king of Judah in the twelfth year of Joram of Israel at age twenty-two and reigns one year in Jerusalem. He walks in the way of Ahab's house and does evil, goes with Joram to war against Hazael at Ramoth Gilead, and visits the wounded Joram in Jezreel.

l: The Second Book of Kings, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 9
s: Elisha the prophet sends a young prophet to Ramoth Gilead to anoint Jehu son of Jehoshaphat as king over Israel, and the young man pronounces the LORD's judgment on the house of Ahab and Jezebel before fleeing. Jehu's fellow captains proclaim him king, and he conspires against Joram and rides to Jezreel, where Joram is recovering from wounds and Ahaziah king of Judah is visiting. Jehu shoots Joram dead on Naboth the Jezreelite's land, and Ahaziah is struck down as he flees and dies at Megiddo. Jehu then goes to Jezreel's gate, where Jezebel taunts him, her eunuchs throw her from the window, and Jehu tramples her. The dogs eat her body so that only her skull, feet, and palms remain, fulfilling the word spoken by Elijah the Tishbite.

l: Elisha, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 9
s: Elisha the prophet calls one of the sons of the prophets and instructs him to take a vial of oil to Ramoth Gilead, anoint Jehu as king over Israel, and flee at once. He gives detailed instructions about finding Jehu and taking him to an inner room.

l: young prophet (son of the prophets sent by Elisha), The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 9
s: The young prophet goes to Ramoth Gilead, singles out Jehu among the captains, and pours oil on his head in an inner room. He announces the LORD's anointing of Jehu and the doom of Ahab's house and Jezebel, then opens the door and flees. Jehu's companions later call him a madman.

l: Jehu, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 9
s: Jehu is anointed king over Israel, acknowledged by the captains who spread their cloaks and blow the trumpet, and conspires against Joram. He drives furiously to Jezreel, kills Joram with an arrow, has Ahaziah pursued and struck, and has Jezebel thrown down and trampled. He then eats and drinks, orders her buried, and cites the LORD's word spoken by Elijah the Tishbite when told her body was mostly gone.

l: LORD, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 9
s: The LORD, through the young prophet, declares Jehu anointed king and commands him to strike Ahab's house to avenge the blood of his servants the prophets. Jehu cites the LORD's earlier word about repaying Ahab for the blood of Naboth and his sons on that plot, and the LORD's word through Elijah about the dogs eating Jezebel.

l: Ahab, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 9
s: Ahab's whole house is declared to be doomed, with every male cut off, and is compared to the houses of Jeroboam son of Nebat and Baasha son of Ahijah. Jehu recalls riding after Ahab with Bidkar and the LORD's burden laid on Ahab for the blood of Naboth and his sons.

l: Ahab's house, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 9
s: The young prophet declares that the whole house of Ahab will perish, like the houses of Jeroboam and Baasha, and that Jehu must strike it to avenge the prophets' blood. Joram, Ahab's son, and Jezebel are killed in this unit.

l: Jezebel, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 9
s: Jezebel is named as the one at whose hand the blood of the LORD's servants was shed, and the prophecy says dogs will eat her at Jezreel with no one to bury her. She paints her eyes, adorns her head, and taunts Jehu from the window, calling him Zimri. Her eunuchs throw her down, Jehu tramples her, and only her skull, feet, and palms are found afterward.

l: Jezreel, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 9
s: Jezreel is where Joram has returned to heal from his wounds and where Ahaziah comes to visit him. Joram and Jezebel are killed there, and Naboth's plot of ground there becomes the place of Joram's body and the fulfillment of the word about Jezebel's remains.

l: Joram, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 9
s: Joram was defending Ramoth Gilead against Hazael king of Syria and returned wounded to Jezreel. He sends two horsemen to ask Jehu if it is peace, then goes out himself, is accused of his mother Jezebel's prostitution and witchcraft, and flees crying treason. Jehu's arrow pierces his heart, and his body is thrown onto Naboth's plot.

l: Ahaziah, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 9
s: Ahaziah king of Judah goes to Jezreel to see Joram and rides out with him to meet Jehu. He flees by the garden house, is struck in his chariot at the ascent of Gur by Ibleam, and dies at Megiddo. His servants carry him to Jerusalem and bury him in David's city.

l: Naboth the Jezreelite, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 9
s: Naboth's land at Jezreel is where Jehu meets Joram and kills him. Jehu has Joram's body thrown onto that plot, citing the LORD's word that he would repay Ahab there for the blood of Naboth and his sons.

l: Jehu's anointing as king, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 9
s: Following Elisha's instructions, the young prophet privately pours oil on Jehu's head at Ramoth Gilead and declares him king over Israel. After Jehu reluctantly repeats the message, the other captains hurry to place their cloaks under him, blow the trumpet, and proclaim him king.

l: Jehu's killing of Joram, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 9
s: After the watchman reports the furious driving, Jehu meets Joram on Naboth's land and answers his question about peace by pointing to Jezebel's prostitution and witchcraft. He draws his bow and shoots Joram through the heart, then has Bidkar throw the body onto Naboth's plot to fulfill the LORD's word.

l: death of Jezebel, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 9
s: Jezebel looks out the window and taunts Jehu, who calls for support and has two or three eunuchs throw her down. Her blood spatters the wall and horses, and Jehu tramples her. When burial is attempted, only her skull, feet, and palms remain, which Jehu says fulfills Elijah's word.

l: The Second Book of Kings, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 10
s: Jehu writes to the rulers and elders of Samaria and Jezreel who raise Ahab's seventy sons, and they, afraid of him, kill the sons and send their heads to Jezreel in baskets. Jehu then kills the remainder of Ahab's house in Jezreel and in Samaria, and kills forty-two brothers of Ahaziah king of Judah at the shearing house pit. He takes Jehonadab the son of Rechab into his chariot, then deceptively gathers all the worshipers of Baal into the house of Baal and has them killed, destroying the house and making it a latrine. The LORD promises Jehu's descendants the throne to the fourth generation, but Jehu does not leave the sins of Jeroboam or walk in the LORD's law, and Hazael begins to strike Israel's eastern territories. Jehu reigns twenty-eight years, dies, and is succeeded by his son Jehoahaz.

l: Jehu, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 10
s: Jehu writes letters to Samaria's leaders, orders the heads of Ahab's sons delivered, and kills the rest of Ahab's house, Ahaziah's brothers, and all of Baal's worshipers through a feigned sacrifice. He destroys Baal out of Israel but does not depart from the golden calves of Jeroboam or walk in the LORD's law. He reigns twenty-eight years, is buried in Samaria, and is succeeded by his son Jehoahaz.

l: Ahab, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 10
s: Ahab is the master whose house Jehu destroys, fulfilling the LORD's word spoken by Elijah. Jehu says Ahab served Baal a little, as part of his ruse to the people.

l: Ahab's sons, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 10
s: Ahab's seventy sons are raised by the great men of Samaria. After Jehu's letters, they are killed and their heads are sent in baskets to Jezreel, where they are laid in two heaps at the gate entrance until morning.

l: Samaria, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 10
s: Samaria is where Ahab's seventy sons are kept and where Jehu's letters are sent. Jehu later strikes all who remained to Ahab there, and he is buried there at his death.

l: Jezreel, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 10
s: Jezreel is where the heads of Ahab's sons are brought and heaped at the gate, and where Jehu addresses the people. There Jehu also strikes the remainder of Ahab's house, great men, friends, and priests.

l: rulers and elders of Jezreel and Samaria, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 10
s: The rulers, elders, and guardians of Ahab's sons, fearing Jehu because two kings could not stand before him, declare themselves his servants and refuse to make any man king. They obey his second letter by killing the seventy sons and sending their heads to him.

l: LORD, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 10
s: The LORD's word against Ahab's house, spoken by Elijah, is said to be fulfilled through Jehu. He promises Jehu's descendants the throne to the fourth generation, and begins cutting away parts of Israel through Hazael's strikes.

l: brothers of Ahaziah, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 10
s: Forty-two brothers of Ahaziah king of Judah, traveling to greet the children of the king and queen, meet Jehu at the shearing house. He orders them taken alive and they are killed at the pit, with none left.

l: Jehonadab the son of Rechab, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 10
s: Jehonadab meets Jehu, affirms that his heart is right with Jehu's, and is taken up into Jehu's chariot to see his zeal for the LORD. He accompanies Jehu into the house of Baal.

l: Baal, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 10
s: Jehu pretends that Ahab served Baal a little but he will serve him much, and calls a great sacrifice to Baal as a deception. Baal's pillar is broken and Jehu is said to destroy Baal out of Israel.

l: worshipers of Baal, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 10
s: All of Baal's prophets, worshipers, and priests are summoned and fill the house of Baal, wearing robes brought out for them. After they offer sacrifices, Jehu's guard and captains kill them all with the sword.

l: house of Baal, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 10
s: The house of Baal is filled from end to end with worshipers, who are killed inside it. Its pillars are burned, and the house is broken down and made a latrine, as it remains to this day.

l: Israel, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 10
s: Israel is purged of Baal worship under Jehu but continues in the sins of Jeroboam, the golden calves at Bethel and Dan. The LORD begins to cut away its territory as Hazael strikes from the Jordan eastward across Gilead and Bashan.

l: Ahab's house massacre, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 10
s: Jehu orchestrates the killing of Ahab's seventy sons by their guardians, then strikes all remaining in Ahab's house at Jezreel and Samaria, leaving none. He tells the people they are righteous and that this fulfills the LORD's word by Elijah.

l: The Second Book of Kings, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 11
s: After Ahaziah's death, Athaliah destroyed the royal offspring, but Jehosheba took Ahaziah's son Joash and hid him with his nurse in the LORD's house for six years while Athaliah reigned. In the seventh year the priest Jehoiada made a covenant with the captains of hundreds of the Carites and the guard, showed them the king's son, and organized them in watches around the king, arming them with David's spears and shields. Jehoiada crowned and anointed Joash, and the people clapped and said, "Long live the king!" Athaliah came to the LORD's house, cried "Treason!", and was led out and slain at the horses' entry to the king's house. Jehoiada made covenants between the LORD, the king, and the people, the people destroyed the house of Baal and killed its priest Mattan, and Joash, seven years old, took the throne while the city was quiet.

l: Athaliah, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 11
s: Athaliah, mother of Ahaziah, destroyed all the royal offspring when her son died and reigned over the land for six years. She heard the noise of the guard and people, came to the LORD's house, tore her clothes and cried "Treason!", and was seized and slain at the horses' entry to the king's house.

l: Jehosheba, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 11
s: Jehosheba, daughter of King Joram and sister of Ahaziah, took Joash from among the slain king's sons and hid him and his nurse in the bedroom. Thanks to her, he was not slain by Athaliah.

l: Jehoash, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 11
s: Joash, son of Ahaziah, was stolen away from the slaughter and hidden in the LORD's house for six years. In the seventh year he was shown to the captains, crowned, given the covenant, anointed, and made king, and he sat on the throne at age seven (called Jehoash).

l: Jehoiada, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 11
s: Jehoiada the priest gathered the captains, made a covenant with them, showed them the king's son, and commanded how the watches were to be set. He supplied David's spears and shields, crowned Joash, ordered Athaliah removed and killed outside the LORD's house, made covenants between the LORD, the king and the people, and appointed officers over the LORD's house.

l: captains over hundreds, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 11
s: The captains over hundreds of the Carites and the guard were fetched by Jehoiada, entered a covenant, and did all he commanded, bringing their men to him. They received David's spears and shields, and were ordered to bring Athaliah out between the ranks and kill anyone who followed her.

l: guard, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 11
s: The guard stood with weapons in hand around the king from the right side of the house to the left, along by the altar. They were commanded to slay anyone entering the ranks, and later helped bring the king down to the king's house by the gate of the guard.

l: people of the land, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 11
s: The people of the land rejoiced and blew trumpets at Joash's coronation. They then went to the house of Baal, broke down its altars and images, and killed Mattan the priest of Baal, and they accompanied the king to his house; the city was quiet.

l: LORD, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 11
s: The LORD is the one to whom Jehoiada's covenant binds the king and the people, so that they should be the LORD's people. His house is the place of Joash's hiding, crowning, and the protection of the king.

l: LORD's house, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 11
s: The LORD's house was where Joash was hidden for six years, where the covenant was made, and where David's spears and shields were kept. Joash was crowned there, and Jehoiada ordered that Athaliah not be slain in it; afterward officers were appointed over it.

l: king's house, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 11
s: The king's house was to be guarded by one third of the incoming watch. Athaliah was slain at the horses' entry to it, and Joash was brought there by the gate of the guard to sit on the throne of the kings.

l: Joash the son of Ahaziah, king of Judah, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 11
s: Jehoiada brought out the king's son, put the crown on him, gave him the covenant, and anointed him while the guard surrounded him. The people clapped and said "Long live the king!", and the king stood by the pillar with captains and trumpets as was the tradition.

l: killing of Athaliah, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 11
s: After Athaliah cried "Treason!", Jehoiada ordered her brought out between the ranks, not to be slain in the LORD's house. She was seized, went by the horses' entry to the king's house, and was slain there with the sword.

l: The Second Book of Kings, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 12
s: Chapter 12 describes Jehoash, who began to reign in the seventh year of Jehu and ruled forty years in Jerusalem, doing right while Jehoiada the priest instructed him, though the high places remained. By Jehoash's twenty-third year the priests had not repaired the damage to the LORD's house, so the king confronted them, and Jehoiada set up a chest beside the altar to collect the money, which was counted and paid to the workers without demanding an accounting. When Hazael king of Syria took Gath and set his face toward Jerusalem, Jehoash sent him the holy things and the gold from the LORD's house and the king's house, and Hazael left. Jehoash's servants Jozacar son of Shimeath and Jehozabad son of Shomer conspired against him and killed him at the house of Millo, and Amaziah his son reigned in his place.

l: Jehoash, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 12
s: Jehoash began to reign in the seventh year of Jehu and reigned forty years in Jerusalem; his mother was Zibiah of Beersheba. He did right all the days Jehoiada instructed him, ordered the money for repairs, and confronted the priests in his twenty-third year when the damage was still unrepaired. He bought off Hazael with the holy things and gold, and was later struck down by his servants at the house of Millo and buried in David's city, with his son Amaziah succeeding him.

l: Jehoiada, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 12
s: Jehoiada the priest instructed Jehoash, who did right in the LORD's eyes all the days of that instruction. When the priests stopped taking money but did not repair the house, Jehoiada took a chest, bored a hole in its lid, and set it beside the altar on the right side as one enters the LORD's house.

l: priests, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 12
s: The priests were told by Jehoash to take the money from their donors and repair the damage to the house, but by his twenty-third year they had not done so. They then consented to take no more money from the people and not repair the house. The priests who kept the threshold put the money brought into the LORD's house into the chest, and the money for trespass and sin offerings remained the priests'.

l: LORD's house, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 12
s: The LORD's house had damage that went unrepaired until after Jehoash's twenty-third year. It was then repaired with money collected in the chest, and no silver cups, snuffers, basins, trumpets, or vessels of gold or silver were made from that money. Later its treasures, along with the king's house treasures, were sent to Hazael.

l: temple repair, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 12
s: Jehoash ordered the priests to repair the damage wherever it was found, but it had not been done by his twenty-third year. Once the chest funds were counted and paid out, carpenters, builders, masons, and stone cutters worked on it, and timber and cut stone were bought. All the money went to the workers and the repair.

l: money (temple donations), The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 12
s: The money brought into the LORD's house included current money, the money from people's evaluations, and whatever anyone chose to bring. Jehoash first directed the priests to take it for repairs, then told them to stop taking it from their treasurers and deliver it for the repair. It was eventually weighed, put in bags, counted, and paid to the workers, while trespass and sin offering money was not brought in and belonged to the priests.

l: chest (Jehoiada's chest), The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 12
s: Jehoiada took a chest and bored a hole in its lid, then set it beside the altar on the right side as one comes into the LORD's house. The threshold-keeping priests put all the money brought to the house into it. When it held much money, the king's scribe and the high priest came up, bagged and counted the money.

l: Hazael, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 12
s: Hazael king of Syria went up, fought against Gath and took it, and set his face to go up to Jerusalem. Jehoash sent him the holy things and gold from the LORD's house and the king's house, and Hazael went away from Jerusalem.

l: holy things and treasures, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 12
s: Jehoash took the holy things dedicated by Jehoshaphat, Jehoram, and Ahaziah, his fathers, along with his own holy things and all the gold in the treasures of the LORD's house and the king's house. He sent all of it to Hazael king of Syria, after which Hazael left Jerusalem.

l: Jehoash's servants, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 12
s: Jehoash's servants arose, made a conspiracy, and struck him at the house of Millo, on the way that goes down to Silla. Two of them are named as Jozacar and Jehozabad.

l: Jozacar, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 12
s: Jozacar the son of Shimeath was one of Jehoash's servants who struck him so that he died.

l: Jehozabad, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 12
s: Jehozabad the son of Shomer was one of Jehoash's servants who struck him so that he died.

l: conspiracy against Jehoash, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 12
s: Jehoash's servants made a conspiracy and struck him at the house of Millo, on the way that goes down to Silla. Jozacar and Jehozabad killed him, he was buried with his fathers in David's city, and Amaziah his son reigned in his place.

l: The Second Book of Kings, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 13
s: Chapter 13 recounts the reigns of Jehoahaz the son of Jehu and his son Jehoash (Joash) over Israel in Samaria. Both did evil and followed the sins of Jeroboam, and under Jehoahaz the LORD delivered Israel to Hazael king of Syria and Benhadad his son until Jehoahaz begged the LORD and a savior was given. Elisha, sick with the illness of which he died, told King Joash to shoot an arrow of victory over Syria and strike the ground; Joash struck only three times, so Elisha said he would defeat Syria just three times. After Elisha died, a man thrown into his tomb revived on touching his bones. Hazael died, Benhadad reigned, and Jehoash defeated Benhadad three times and recovered Israel's cities, as the LORD showed grace because of his covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.

l: Jehoahaz the son of Jehu, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 13
s: Jehoahaz began to reign over Israel in Samaria in the twenty-third year of Joash of Judah and reigned seventeen years. He did evil and followed the sins of Jeroboam, and the LORD delivered Israel into the hands of Hazael and Benhadad. He begged the LORD, who listened, and he was left with only fifty horsemen, ten chariots, and ten thousand footmen. He slept with his fathers, was buried in Samaria, and was succeeded by his son Joash.

l: Jehoash the son of Jehoahaz, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 13
s: Jehoash (also called Joash) began to reign over Israel in Samaria in the thirty-seventh year of Joash of Judah and reigned sixteen years, doing evil and walking in the sins of Jeroboam. He fought Amaziah king of Judah, wept over the sick Elisha, and struck the ground only three times at Elisha's command, drawing Elisha's anger. He struck Benhadad three times and recovered the cities of Israel, then slept with his fathers and was buried in Samaria while Jeroboam sat on his throne.

l: LORD, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 13
s: The LORD's anger burned against Israel and he delivered them to Hazael and Benhadad, yet he listened to Jehoahaz's plea and gave Israel a savior. He was gracious and compassionate to Israel because of his covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and had not yet destroyed them or cast them from his presence. The arrow Elisha had the king shoot was called the LORD's arrow of victory over Syria.

l: Israel, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 13
s: Israel was oppressed by Syria under Hazael and Benhadad because of its sins, but was given a savior and lived in its tents as before. It did not depart from the sins of the house of Jeroboam, and the Asherah remained in Samaria. The LORD favored it because of his covenant, and Jehoash recovered its cities from Benhadad.

l: Hazael, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 13
s: Hazael king of Syria oppressed Israel all the days of Jehoahaz, with the LORD delivering Israel into his hand. He died and his son Benhadad reigned in his place.

l: Benhadad the son of Hazael, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 13
s: Benhadad was given power over Israel along with his father Hazael, and he reigned after Hazael died. Jehoash took back from him the cities that had been taken from Jehoahaz, striking him three times.

l: Syria, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 13
s: Syria oppressed Israel under Hazael, and its king destroyed Jehoahaz's forces, making them like dust in threshing. Elisha foretold that Israel would strike the Syrians at Aphek, and because the king struck the ground only three times, Syria would be defeated just three times. Jehoash then struck Benhadad three times.

l: Elisha, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 13
s: Elisha became sick with the illness of which he died, and King Joash wept over him, calling him "My father, my father, the chariots of Israel and its horsemen!" He had the king shoot an arrow eastward as the LORD's arrow of victory over Syria, then grew angry when the king struck the ground only three times, saying he should have struck five or six. Elisha died and was buried, and a man touching his bones later revived.

l: man (revived by Elisha's bones), The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 13
s: As this man was being buried, the burial party saw a band of raiders and threw him into Elisha's tomb. As soon as he touched Elisha's bones, he revived and stood up on his feet.

l: The Second Book of Kings, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 14
s: Chapter 14 recounts the reign of Amaziah, who became king of Judah at twenty-five in the second year of Joash of Israel and did right but not like David, leaving the high places in place. He executed the servants who had killed his father but spared their children, and he struck down ten thousand Edomites and took Sela. Emboldened, he challenged Jehoash king of Israel, who answered with a parable of a thistle and a cedar; Judah was defeated at Beth Shemesh, Amaziah was captured, Jerusalem's wall was broken down for four hundred cubits, and the temple and royal treasures were taken to Samaria. Jehoash died and was succeeded by Jeroboam, and Amaziah later fled a conspiracy to Lachish, where he was killed, after which Azariah, aged sixteen, became king. Jeroboam son of Joash reigned forty-one years in Samaria, did evil, yet restored Israel's borders as spoken by the prophet Jonah son of Amittai, and was succeeded by his son Zechariah.

l: Amaziah, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 14
s: Amaziah began to reign at twenty-five and reigned twenty-nine years in Jerusalem, doing right but not like David, and he killed his father's murderers while sparing their children. He struck ten thousand Edomites, then provoked Jehoash of Israel, ignored his warning, was defeated and captured at Beth Shemesh. He outlived Jehoash by fifteen years, fled a conspiracy to Lachish, was killed there, and was buried in Jerusalem; Azariah succeeded him.

l: Jehoash the son of Jehoahaz, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 14
s: Jehoash answered Amaziah's challenge with a parable of a thistle and a cedar, warning him to stay home. He defeated Judah at Beth Shemesh, took Amaziah, broke down part of Jerusalem's wall, carried off gold, silver, vessels and hostages to Samaria, and then died and was buried in Samaria, succeeded by his son Jeroboam.

l: Jeroboam the son of Joash king of Israel, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 14
s: Jeroboam began to reign in Samaria in the fifteenth year of Amaziah and reigned forty-one years, doing evil and not departing from the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat. He restored Israel's border from Hamath to the sea of the Arabah according to the word spoken through the prophet Jonah son of Amittai, and recovered Damascus and Hamath. He was succeeded by his son Zechariah.

l: Judah, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 14
s: Judah, under Amaziah, was defeated by Israel at Beth Shemesh, and each man fled to his tent. After Amaziah was killed in a conspiracy, all the people of Judah made sixteen-year-old Azariah king in his place.

l: Israel, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 14
s: Israel under Jehoash defeated Judah at Beth Shemesh and plundered Jerusalem. Under Jeroboam, the LORD saw Israel's bitter affliction and saved it by his hand rather than blotting out its name, and its borders were restored.

l: Jerusalem, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 14
s: Jerusalem was entered by Jehoash, who broke down its wall from the gate of Ephraim to the corner gate, four hundred cubits, and took treasures from the LORD's house and the king's house. Amaziah reigned there, and he was later brought back on horses and buried in David's city.

l: Beth Shemesh, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 14
s: Beth Shemesh, which belongs to Judah, was the place where Jehoash and Amaziah met face to face. There Judah was defeated and Jehoash took Amaziah captive.

l: battle at Beth Shemesh (Amaziah and Jehoash), The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 14
s: After Amaziah refused Jehoash's warning, the two kings faced each other at Beth Shemesh. Judah was defeated by Israel and each man fled to his tent, and Amaziah was captured, leading to Jerusalem's wall being broken and its treasures taken.

l: The Second Book of Kings, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 15
s: Chapter 15 traces the kings of Judah and Israel. Azariah of Judah reigns fifty-two years, is struck with leprosy by the LORD, and is succeeded by his son Jotham, who also does right but leaves the high places standing. In Israel a rapid series of kings follows: Zechariah is killed by Shallum, Shallum by Menahem, Menahem is succeeded by Pekahiah, Pekahiah is killed by Pekah, and Pekah is killed by Hoshea. During this period Assyria intervenes, with Pul receiving silver from Menahem and Tiglath Pileser capturing northern territories and carrying people captive under Pekah. Near the end, the LORD begins sending Rezin of Syria and Pekah against Judah, and Jotham is succeeded by Ahaz.

l: Azariah, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 15
s: Azariah son of Amaziah began to reign in Judah at sixteen and reigned fifty-two years in Jerusalem. He did right in the LORD's eyes but did not remove the high places. The LORD struck him with leprosy, so he lived in a separate house until he died, and his son Jotham was over the household; Jotham then succeeded him.

l: Israel, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 15
s: Israel saw a rapid succession of kings: Zechariah, Shallum, Menahem, Pekahiah, and Pekah, with Hoshea killing Pekah and taking the throne. Menahem exacted fifty shekels of silver from each wealthy man in Israel to pay Assyria. Tiglath Pileser took northern lands of Israel and carried their people captive to Assyria.

l: LORD, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 15
s: The LORD struck King Azariah with leprosy until his death. The text notes that his word to Jehu, that his sons to the fourth generation would sit on Israel's throne, was fulfilled in Zechariah. Near the end of the chapter, the LORD began sending Rezin of Syria and Pekah against Judah.

l: Jotham, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 15
s: Jotham was over the household and judged the people while his father Azariah was leprous. He began to reign at twenty-five in the second year of Pekah and reigned sixteen years, doing right but leaving the high places, and he built the upper gate of the LORD's house. He died and was succeeded by his son Ahaz.

l: Zechariah, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 15
s: Zechariah son of Jeroboam reigned over Israel in Samaria for six months and did evil, following the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat. Shallum conspired against him, struck him before the people, and killed him.

l: Shallum, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 15
s: Shallum son of Jabesh conspired against Zechariah, killed him, and reigned in Samaria for one month. Menahem son of Gadi came from Tirzah, killed him, and reigned in his place.

l: Menahem, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 15
s: Menahem son of Gadi killed Shallum and reigned ten years in Samaria, doing evil. He attacked Tiphsah for not opening its gates and ripped up its pregnant women. He gave Pul of Assyria a thousand talents of silver, raised by taxing wealthy men fifty shekels each, and was succeeded by his son Pekahiah.

l: Pekahiah, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 15
s: Pekahiah son of Menahem reigned two years over Israel in Samaria and did evil. His captain Pekah conspired against him and killed him in the fortress of the king's house, then reigned in his place.

l: Pekah, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 15
s: Pekah son of Remaliah, captain of Pekahiah, killed him and reigned twenty years in Samaria, doing evil. Tiglath Pileser of Assyria took many northern lands during his reign. Hoshea conspired against and killed him, and the LORD began sending him with Rezin of Syria against Judah.

l: Tiglath Pileser, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 15
s: Tiglath Pileser king of Assyria came in the days of Pekah and took Ijon, Abel Beth Maacah, Janoah, Kedesh, Hazor, Gilead, and Galilee, all the land of Naphtali. He carried the people captive to Assyria.

l: Hoshea, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 15
s: Hoshea son of Elah conspired against Pekah son of Remaliah, attacked and killed him, and reigned in his place. This happened in the twentieth year of Jotham.

l: The Second Book of Kings, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 16
s: Chapter 16 describes Ahaz son of Jotham, who became king of Judah at twenty and reigned sixteen years in Jerusalem, doing evil by following the kings of Israel, making his son pass through the fire, and sacrificing at the high places. Rezin king of Syria and Pekah king of Israel besieged Jerusalem but could not overcome Ahaz, though Rezin recovered Elath for Syria. Ahaz sent silver and gold from the LORD's house and the king's treasuries to Tiglath Pileser king of Assyria, who took Damascus, carried its people to Kir, and killed Rezin. Ahaz then saw the altar at Damascus and had Urijah the priest build a copy, which Ahaz used for offerings while moving the bronze altar aside and stripping parts of the temple furnishings because of the king of Assyria. Ahaz died and was buried in David's city, and his son Hezekiah reigned in his place.

l: Ahaz, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 16
s: Ahaz became king of Judah at twenty, reigned sixteen years in Jerusalem, and did not do right in the LORD's eyes, making his son pass through the fire and sacrificing at the high places. He bought the help of Assyria with silver and gold from the LORD's house, copied the Damascus altar, set aside the bronze altar, and altered the temple furnishings because of the king of Assyria. He died and was buried in David's city, succeeded by his son Hezekiah.

l: Pekah, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 16
s: Pekah son of Remaliah, king of Israel, is named as the reference point for the start of Ahaz's reign, in his seventeenth year. He joined Rezin king of Syria in coming up to Jerusalem to wage war and besieging Ahaz, but they could not overcome him.

l: Rezin, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 16
s: Rezin king of Syria came up against Jerusalem with Pekah and besieged Ahaz without overcoming him. He recovered Elath for Syria and drove the Jews out, so that Syrians lived there to this day. He was killed when the king of Assyria took Damascus.

l: Tiglath Pileser, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 16
s: Tiglath Pileser king of Assyria was called on by Ahaz, who described himself as his servant and son, and was sent a present of silver and gold. He listened, went up against Damascus, took it, carried its people captive to Kir, and killed Rezin. Ahaz met him at Damascus, and Ahaz's later changes to the temple were made because of him.

l: Urijah, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 16
s: Urijah the priest received from Ahaz a drawing and plans of the Damascus altar and built a matching altar before Ahaz returned from Damascus. He then did as Ahaz commanded, offering the regular sacrifices on the great altar.

l: Jerusalem, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 16
s: Jerusalem was where Ahaz reigned sixteen years. Rezin and Pekah came up to it to wage war and besieged it, but could not overcome Ahaz.

l: Damascus, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 16
s: Damascus was taken by the king of Assyria, who carried its people captive to Kir and killed Rezin. Ahaz went there to meet Tiglath Pileser and saw the altar that was there.

l: altar at Damascus, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 16
s: Ahaz saw this altar at Damascus and sent Urijah a drawing and plans to build one like it. Urijah built it before Ahaz returned, and Ahaz offered his burnt, meal, drink and peace offerings on it. It became the great altar for the morning and evening offerings and those of all the people of the land.

l: bronze altar, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 16
s: The bronze altar, which stood before the LORD, was moved by Ahaz from the front of the house, from between his new altar and the LORD's house, to the north side of his altar. Ahaz said it would be for him to inquire by.

l: idolatrous worship, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 16
s: Ahaz walked in the way of the kings of Israel, made his son pass through the fire according to the abominations of the nations, and sacrificed and burned incense on the high places, on hills and under every green tree. The text also records him replacing the arrangement of temple worship with an altar copied from Damascus.

l: The Second Book of Kings, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 17
s: Hoshea the son of Elah becomes king of Israel in Samaria, rules nine years, and does evil, though less than earlier kings. Shalmaneser king of Assyria makes him a tributary, then imprisons him after discovering that Hoshea sent messengers to So king of Egypt and withheld tribute. The king of Assyria besieges Samaria for three years and takes it in Hoshea's ninth year, carrying Israel off to Halah, the Habor, and the cities of the Medes. The text explains this as the LORD's judgment for Israel's idolatry, child sacrifice, high places, and rejection of the prophets' warnings, and notes that Judah also followed Israel's ways. The king of Assyria then resettles Samaria with people from Babylon, Cuthah, Avva, Hamath, and Sepharvaim, who are attacked by lions, are taught to fear the LORD by a returned priest, yet keep serving their own gods.

l: Hoshea, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 17
s: Hoshea began to reign over Israel in Samaria in the twelfth year of Ahaz of Judah and ruled nine years, doing evil but not as badly as earlier kings. He became Shalmaneser's servant and paid tribute, but then sent messengers to So king of Egypt and stopped the tribute. The king of Assyria seized him and bound him in prison.

l: Shalmaneser king of Assyria, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 17
s: Shalmaneser came up against Hoshea and made him a tribute-paying servant. When he discovered Hoshea's conspiracy with So king of Egypt and the withheld tribute, the king of Assyria seized and imprisoned Hoshea.

l: Israel, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 17
s: Israel is carried away to Assyria and settled in Halah, on the Habor, and in the cities of the Medes because it sinned against the LORD. It feared other gods, followed the nations' practices, built high places, made two calves, an Asherah, and served Baal, passed children through fire, and walked in the sins of Jeroboam. It ignored every prophet's warning, and the LORD removed it from his sight, leaving only Judah.

l: Judah, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 17
s: Judah was warned by the LORD along with Israel through every prophet and seer. It is left as the only remaining tribe after Israel's removal, but it also failed to keep the LORD's commandments and walked in the statutes Israel made.

l: LORD, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 17
s: The LORD, who brought Israel out of Egypt, is shown as angered by Israel's idolatry and as having warned Israel and Judah through the prophets to turn back. He removed Israel from his sight as he had said, and later sent lions among the foreign settlers who did not fear him. The text recalls his covenant command to fear only him and promise to deliver them from all enemies.

l: Assyria, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 17
s: Assyria's king besieges and captures Samaria, deports Israel to Halah, the Habor, and the cities of the Medes, and replaces them with peoples from Babylon, Cuthah, Avva, Hamath, and Sepharvaim. When the settlers suffer lions, he orders one of the exiled priests sent back to teach them the law of the god of the land.

l: Samaria, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 17
s: Samaria, Hoshea's capital, is besieged for three years by the king of Assyria and taken in Hoshea's ninth year. Its cities are then occupied by foreign settlers brought by Assyria in place of the Israelites, and its high places house their gods.

l: foreign settlers in Samaria, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 17
s: People from Babylon, Cuthah, Avva, Hamath, and Sepharvaim are placed in Samaria's cities. They did not fear the LORD at first, so lions killed some of them, and a returned priest living at Bethel taught them to fear him. They also kept making their own gods, such as Succoth Benoth, Nergal, Ashima, Nibhaz, Tartak, Adrammelech, and Anammelech, and appointed priests of the high places. They and their descendants keep this mixed worship to this day.

l: idolatry and high-place worship, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 17
s: Israel built high places in all its cities, set up pillars and Asherah poles, burned incense, served idols, made molten calves, worshiped the sky's army and Baal, and sacrificed children, all of which the text gives as the reason for its exile. The foreign settlers repeat the pattern by placing their own gods in the high-place houses and appointing priests for them, while also fearing the LORD.

l: siege and fall of Samaria, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 17
s: After finding Hoshea's conspiracy, the king of Assyria came up through the land and besieged Samaria for three years. He took it in Hoshea's ninth year.

l: exile of Israel to Assyria, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 17
s: In the ninth year of Hoshea, the king of Assyria carried Israel away and placed them in Halah, on the Habor, the river of Gozan, and in the cities of the Medes. The text presents this as the fulfillment of what the LORD said through his prophets, and says Israel remains carried away to this day.

l: The Second Book of Kings, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 18
s: Chapter 18 introduces Hezekiah, who began to reign over Judah in the third year of Hoshea, did right in the LORD's eyes, removed the high places, broke the bronze serpent Nehushtan, trusted the LORD, prospered, and rebelled against Assyria. It recounts how Shalmaneser king of Assyria besieged and took Samaria and carried Israel away to Assyria because they disobeyed the LORD and transgressed his covenant. In Hezekiah's fourteenth year, Sennacherib took Judah's fortified cities, and Hezekiah paid him silver and gold, stripping the temple doors and pillars. Sennacherib then sent Tartan, Rabsaris, and Rabshakeh with a great army to Jerusalem, where Rabshakeh mocked Hezekiah's trust in Egypt and the LORD and urged the people to surrender. The people stayed silent as the king commanded, and Eliakim, Shebna, and Joah returned to Hezekiah with torn clothes to report his words.

l: Hezekiah, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 18
s: Hezekiah son of Ahaz began to reign over Judah at twenty-five, reigned twenty-nine years, and did right in the LORD's eyes by removing the high places, breaking the pillars, cutting down the Asherah, and breaking the bronze serpent Nehushtan. He trusted the LORD, prospered, rebelled against Assyria, and struck the Philistines to Gaza. When Sennacherib took Judah's fortified cities, he sent to him at Lachish, admitted offense, and paid three hundred talents of silver and thirty of gold, stripping the temple and palace treasuries and the temple's gold doors and pillars. He then received the report of Rabshakeh's words from his officials.

l: LORD, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 18
s: The LORD was with Hezekiah, who trusted him, kept his commandments given through Moses, and prospered wherever he went. Israel was carried away because they did not obey the LORD's voice and transgressed his covenant. Rabshakeh claimed the LORD had told him to go up against the land and destroy it, and argued that the LORD could not deliver Jerusalem, as no other nation's gods had delivered theirs.

l: Jerusalem, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 18
s: Jerusalem was approached by a great Assyrian army sent from Lachish, which stood by the conduit of the upper pool on the highway of the fuller's field. Rabshakeh demanded the city's surrender and shouted to the people on the wall, but they stayed silent. Hezekiah's officials had paid tribute from the city's temple and palace treasures before this.

l: Sennacherib, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 18
s: Sennacherib, king of Assyria, came up in Hezekiah's fourteenth year against all of Judah's fortified cities and took them. He appointed three hundred talents of silver and thirty talents of gold from Hezekiah and received the temple and palace silver and gold. He then sent Tartan, Rabsaris, and Rabshakeh with a great army from Lachish to Jerusalem.

l: Rabshakeh, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 18
s: Rabshakeh, sent with Tartan and Rabsaris by the king of Assyria, stood by the upper pool conduit and spoke to Eliakim, Shebnah, and Joah. He refused their request to speak in the Syrian language and instead cried out in the Jews' language to the people on the wall. He mocked Hezekiah's trust in Egypt and the LORD and offered the people peace and resettlement if they surrendered.

l: Eliakim, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 18
s: Eliakim son of Hilkiah, who was over the household, went out with Shebnah the scribe and Joah the recorder to meet Rabshakeh. He asked Rabshakeh to speak in the Syrian language rather than the Jews' language in the hearing of the people on the wall. Afterward he came to Hezekiah with torn clothes and reported Rabshakeh's words.

l: Rabshakeh's speech, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 18
s: Rabshakeh's speech argued that Hezekiah's confidence was vain, that Egypt was a bruised reed that pierces the hand, and that Hezekiah had removed the LORD's high places and altars. It offered two thousand horses if Judah could supply riders, claimed the LORD had commanded Assyria to destroy the land, and urged the people to make peace and not listen to Hezekiah. It cited the fallen gods of Hamath, Arpad, Sepharvaim, Hena, Ivvah, and Samaria as proof the LORD could not deliver Jerusalem; the people answered nothing.

l: The Second Book of Kings, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 19
s: King Hezekiah of Judah, hearing Rabshakeh's taunts, tears his clothes, puts on sackcloth, and sends Eliakim, Shebna, and the priests' elders to Isaiah, who answers that the LORD will make the king of Assyria hear news and fall by the sword in his own land. Sennacherib, king of Assyria, then sends Hezekiah a threatening letter claiming no god has saved any nation from Assyria. Hezekiah spreads the letter before the LORD and prays for deliverance so all kingdoms will know the LORD alone is God. Isaiah relays the LORD's reply: Sennacherib's arrogance will be punished, he will be turned back by the way he came, and he will not enter or shoot an arrow at Jerusalem. That night the LORD's angel strikes 185,000 in the Assyrian camp, Sennacherib returns to Nineveh, and his sons Adrammelech and Sharezer kill him while he worships in the house of Nisroch, after which Esar Haddon reigns.

l: Hezekiah, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 19
s: Hezekiah tears his clothes, puts on sackcloth, goes to the LORD's house, and sends messengers to Isaiah asking for prayer for the remnant. After receiving Sennacherib's letter, he spreads it before the LORD and prays for deliverance. He is rewarded with the LORD's promise to defend Jerusalem, and the Assyrian threat ends.

l: LORD, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 19
s: The LORD, through Isaiah, promises that the Assyrian king will hear news, return home, and fall by the sword, and says he has heard Hezekiah's prayer. He declares he will put his hook in Sennacherib's nose and turn him back, and that he will defend Jerusalem for his own sake and David's sake. He then sends his angel to strike the Assyrian camp.

l: Isaiah, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 19
s: Isaiah, son of Amoz, receives Hezekiah's messengers and tells them not to be afraid, since the LORD will make the Assyrian king return home and die by the sword. He later sends Hezekiah a longer message of the LORD's answer, including a rebuke of Sennacherib, a sign of recovery over three years, and a promise that Assyria will not take the city.

l: Sennacherib, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 19
s: Sennacherib, king of Assyria, sends messengers with a letter defying the LORD and claiming no god has saved nations from Assyria. The LORD rebukes his arrogance and promises to turn him back. He departs, lives at Nineveh, and is killed by his sons Adrammelech and Sharezer while worshiping in the house of Nisroch his god.

l: Rabshakeh, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 19
s: Rabshakeh is the Assyrian envoy whose words defying the living God alarm Hezekiah. He returns to find the king of Assyria warring against Libnah, having heard the king had left Lachish.

l: Assyria, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 19
s: Assyria's king and servants are said to have blasphemed the LORD, and its kings are described as having laid waste nations and burned their gods. Its king hears of Tirhakah king of Ethiopia coming out to fight and sends a threatening letter to Hezekiah. Its camp is struck by the LORD's angel with 185,000 dead, and its king returns home and is later assassinated, with Esar Haddon his son reigning in his place.

l: Jerusalem, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 19
s: Jerusalem is threatened by Assyria but the LORD promises the king of Assyria will not enter it, shoot an arrow there, or build a mound against it. The LORD says he will defend the city for his own sake and for David's sake. A remnant is promised to go out from it and from Mount Zion.

l: the LORD's angel, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 19
s: The LORD's angel goes out in the night and strikes 185,000 in the Assyrian camp. By morning they are all dead bodies.

l: slaughter of the Assyrian camp, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 19
s: In one night the LORD's angel strikes 185,000 in the Assyrian camp, and when men rise early in the morning they find all were dead bodies. It fulfills the promise that the Assyrian king would not take Jerusalem, and Sennacherib then departs and goes home to Nineveh.

l: Hezekiah's prayer, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 19
s: In the LORD's house Hezekiah addresses the LORD as God of Israel, enthroned above the cherubim, and sole God of all kingdoms who made heaven and earth. He asks him to hear Sennacherib's words and save them so all kingdoms will know the LORD alone is God. The LORD answers through Isaiah that he has heard the prayer.

l: The Second Book of Kings, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 20
s: Hezekiah, sick and dying, is told by the prophet Isaiah that the LORD says he will die, but after Hezekiah prays and weeps, the LORD sends Isaiah back to promise healing, fifteen more years, and deliverance of the city from the king of Assyria. Isaiah has a cake of figs laid on the boil, and Hezekiah recovers. As a sign, the LORD, at Isaiah's cry, makes the shadow go back ten steps on the sundial of Ahaz, as Hezekiah chose. Berodach Baladan, king of Babylon, sends letters and a present, and Hezekiah shows the envoys all his treasures and armor. Isaiah rebukes this, prophesying that everything will be carried to Babylon and some of Hezekiah's sons will become eunuchs there; Hezekiah calls the word good, hoping for peace and truth in his days, and he later dies and is succeeded by his son Manasseh.

l: Hezekiah, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 20
s: Hezekiah, sick and dying, prays and weeps, and is granted healing and fifteen more years. He chooses the shadow going back ten steps as the sign, then shows Babylon's envoys all his treasures and armor. After hearing Isaiah's prophecy of Babylonian plunder, he calls it good and hopes for peace and truth in his days; he dies and his son Manasseh reigns in his place.

l: Isaiah, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 20
s: Isaiah the prophet, son of Amoz, first delivers the LORD's word that Hezekiah will die, then is sent back to announce healing and fifteen added years. He has a cake of figs applied to the boil and cries to the LORD so the shadow goes back ten steps. He later questions Hezekiah about the Babylonian envoys and prophesies that all in the house will be carried to Babylon and some sons made eunuchs.

l: LORD, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 20
s: The LORD tells Hezekiah through Isaiah to set his house in order, then hears his prayer and sees his tears and reverses the verdict. He promises healing, fifteen more years, deliverance from the king of Assyria, and defense of the city for his own and David's sake. He brings the shadow back ten steps as a sign and declares that everything in Hezekiah's house will be carried to Babylon.

l: Berodach Baladan, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 20
s: Berodach Baladan, son of Baladan and king of Babylon, sends letters and a present to Hezekiah after hearing he had been sick.

l: Babylon, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 20
s: Babylon is a far country whose king sends envoys to Hezekiah. Isaiah prophesies that all the contents of Hezekiah's house and the treasures stored by his fathers will be carried there, and that some of Hezekiah's sons will be eunuchs in the king of Babylon's palace.

l: Babylonian envoys (sent by Berodach Baladan), The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 20
s: The envoys bring letters and a present from Berodach Baladan to Hezekiah. Hezekiah listens to them and shows them his storehouse, silver, gold, spices, precious oil, armory, and everything in his treasures and dominion.

l: Hezekiah's sickness (boil), The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 20
s: Hezekiah's illness is first declared fatal by Isaiah. After his prayer, the LORD promises healing, and a cake of figs laid on the boil leads to his recovery. He is promised he will go up to the LORD's house on the third day.

l: Hezekiah's treasures, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 20
s: Hezekiah's treasures include silver, gold, spices, precious oil, his armory, and everything in his storehouses, all of which he shows to the Babylonian envoys. Isaiah prophesies that all of it, along with what his fathers stored, will be carried to Babylon with nothing left.

l: The Second Book of Kings, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 21
s: Chapter 21 describes Manasseh, who became king of Judah at age twelve and reigned fifty-five years in Jerusalem, doing evil by rebuilding the high places, raising altars for Baal and the army of the sky, making an Asherah, and practicing child sacrifice and sorcery. He placed altars and the Asherah image in the LORD's house and shed much innocent blood, leading Judah into worse evil than the nations the LORD had destroyed. The LORD, speaking through the prophets, declared he would bring disaster on Jerusalem and Judah, wiping Jerusalem like a dish and giving the remnant of his inheritance to their enemies. Manasseh died and was buried in the garden of Uzza, and his son Amon reigned two years, following his father's evil ways and abandoning the LORD. Amon's servants conspired and killed him in his house, but the people of the land killed the conspirators and made his son Josiah king.

l: Manasseh, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 21
s: Manasseh became king of Judah at twelve and reigned fifty-five years in Jerusalem, doing evil by rebuilding high places, raising altars for Baal and the army of the sky, making an Asherah, passing his son through the fire, practicing sorcery, and shedding much innocent blood. He seduced Judah to do more evil than the nations the LORD destroyed, and the LORD pronounced judgment because of him. He died, was buried in the garden of Uzza, and was succeeded by his son Amon.

l: Amon, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 21
s: Amon, son of Manasseh and Meshullemeth, became king at twenty-two and reigned two years in Jerusalem. He did evil as his father had, served his father's idols, and abandoned the LORD. His servants conspired against him and killed him in his own house, and he was buried in the garden of Uzza, succeeded by his son Josiah.

l: LORD, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 21
s: The LORD is described as having chosen Jerusalem as the place for his name and as having promised that Israel would not wander from the land if they obeyed his law. Offended by Manasseh's evil, he spoke through the prophets to announce disaster on Jerusalem and Judah, saying he would cast off the remnant of his inheritance to their enemies. Amon also abandoned him.

l: Jerusalem, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 21
s: Jerusalem, where Manasseh and Amon reigned, is the city the LORD chose to put his name, yet Manasseh filled it with innocent blood from one end to the other. The LORD declares he will stretch over it the line of Samaria and the plumb line of Ahab's house and wipe it like a dish, turning it upside down.

l: Judah, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 21
s: Judah was led by Manasseh to sin with idols and to do evil more than the nations the LORD destroyed. The LORD announces that such evil will come on Judah that the ears of all who hear of it will tingle. Its kings Manasseh and Amon are recorded in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Judah.

l: Israel, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 21
s: Israel is referred to as the people whom the LORD brought out of Egypt and for whom he cast out the nations from the land. The LORD had promised David and Solomon that he would not make Israel's feet wander from the land if they kept his law, and says that the people have provoked him since leaving Egypt. Ahab, king of Israel, is cited as a model for Manasseh's idolatry.

l: LORD's house, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 21
s: Manasseh built altars for all the army of the sky in the two courts of the LORD's house, which the LORD had said would bear his name forever. He also set the engraved image of Asherah in it, defiling the place the LORD had chosen.

l: servants of Amon, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 21
s: The servants of Amon conspired against him and put the king to death in his own house. The people of the land then killed all of those who had conspired.

l: people of the land, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 21
s: The people of the land killed all who had conspired against King Amon. They then made Amon's son Josiah king in his place.

l: coming judgment on Jerusalem and Judah, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 21
s: Because of Manasseh's abominations and his leading Judah into sin, the LORD announces through his prophets a disaster so severe that the ears of all who hear will tingle. He will stretch over Jerusalem the line of Samaria and the plumb line of Ahab's house, wipe it like a dish, and give the remnant of his inheritance to enemies as prey and plunder. The reason given is that the people have provoked him since the day their fathers came out of Egypt.

l: The Second Book of Kings, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 22
s: Josiah becomes king of Judah at age eight, reigns thirty-one years in Jerusalem, and does what is right in the LORD's eyes, following David. In his eighteenth year he sends Shaphan the scribe to Hilkiah the high priest to arrange counting and delivering money to the workers repairing the LORD's house. Hilkiah announces he has found the book of the law, and Shaphan reads it to the king, who tears his clothes. Josiah sends Hilkiah, Ahikam, Achbor, Shaphan, and Asaiah to inquire of the LORD through the prophetess Huldah. She declares that the LORD will bring evil on Jerusalem and its people for forsaking him and burning incense to other gods, but that Josiah, because he humbled himself, will be gathered to his grave in peace and not see the evil.

l: Josiah, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 22
s: Josiah became king at age eight and reigned thirty-one years in Jerusalem, doing right and following David. After hearing the book of the law he tore his clothes and sent officials to inquire of the LORD. Through Huldah he learns that because his heart was tender and he humbled himself, he will die in peace and not see the coming evil.

l: LORD, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 22
s: The LORD, through Huldah, declares he will bring evil on this place and its inhabitants because they forsook him and burned incense to other gods, and his wrath will not be quenched. He says he heard Josiah, who humbled himself and wept, and promises him burial in peace.

l: Shaphan, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 22
s: Shaphan the scribe, son of Azaliah, is sent by Josiah to Hilkiah about the money for the LORD's house. He receives the book of the law from Hilkiah, reads it, reports to the king, and reads it before him. He is also one of those sent to inquire of Huldah.

l: Hilkiah, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 22
s: Hilkiah the high priest is to count the money brought into the LORD's house. He announces finding the book of the law and delivers it to Shaphan. He is later sent by the king with others to inquire of the LORD through Huldah.

l: LORD's house, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 22
s: The LORD's house needs repair, and money gathered by the keepers of the threshold is delivered to the workers overseeing it. In it Hilkiah finds the book of the law.

l: book of the covenant, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 22
s: The book of the law is found by Hilkiah in the LORD's house and read by Shaphan, first to himself and then before the king. Its words cause Josiah to tear his clothes and conclude that the LORD's wrath is kindled because their fathers did not obey what it says. Huldah confirms the evil in it will come on the place.

l: temple repair, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 22
s: Josiah orders money to be given to the workers overseeing the LORD's house for carpenters, builders, masons, and for timber and cut stone. No accounting is required of them because they deal faithfully. The discovery of the book occurs in the course of this work.

l: Huldah, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 22
s: Huldah the prophetess, wife of Shallum and living in Jerusalem's second quarter, is consulted by Hilkiah, Ahikam, Achbor, Shaphan, and Asaiah. She delivers the LORD's word of coming evil on the place and a separate promise of peace for Josiah.

l: Judah, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 22
s: Judah and its people are included in Josiah's inquiry because the LORD's wrath is kindled against them for their fathers' disobedience to the book. The LORD says evil will come on this place and its inhabitants because they forsook him and burned incense to other gods.

l: God's coming judgment, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 22
s: The LORD, through Huldah, declares he will bring evil on Jerusalem and its inhabitants, matching all the words of the book, and his wrath will not be quenched. The cause is that they forsook him and burned incense to other gods. Josiah is spared from seeing it because of his humility.

l: The Second Book of Kings, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 23
s: King Josiah gathers the elders, priests, prophets, and people of Judah and Jerusalem, reads them the book of the covenant found in the LORD's house, and makes a covenant before the LORD. He then purges Judah, Jerusalem, Bethel, and the cities of Samaria of idolatrous objects, priests, altars, and high places, and commands the people to keep a Passover unlike any before it. Although no king before or after him turned to the LORD as he did, the LORD does not turn from his wrath over Manasseh's provocations and says he will remove Judah and cast off Jerusalem. Josiah is killed at Megiddo by Pharaoh Necoh, and the people of the land make his son Jehoahaz king. Necoh binds Jehoahaz, who dies in Egypt, places Eliakim on the throne as Jehoiakim, and imposes a tribute on the land, and both kings are described as doing evil in the LORD's sight.

l: Josiah, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 23
s: Josiah gathers the people, reads them the book of the covenant, and makes a covenant before the LORD to keep his commandments with all his heart and soul. He destroys idolatrous objects and high places, kills the priests of the high places in Samaria, and commands the Passover. He is described as unmatched among kings in turning to the LORD, but Pharaoh Necoh kills him at Megiddo, and he is buried in his own tomb in Jerusalem.

l: LORD, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 23
s: The LORD is the one before whom Josiah makes the covenant and for whom the Passover is kept. Despite Josiah's devotion, he does not turn from his great wrath against Judah because of Manasseh's provocation, and he declares he will remove Judah from his sight as he removed Israel and cast off Jerusalem, the city he chose. He sees Jehoahaz and Jehoiakim as doing evil.

l: book of the covenant, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 23
s: The book of the covenant, found in the LORD's house, is read aloud by the king to all the people. Its words are confirmed by the covenant Josiah makes, and the Passover is kept as it is written in it. Josiah's removal of spirit-mediums, wizards, teraphim, and idols is also done to confirm the law written in the book Hilkiah found.

l: Judah, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 23
s: Judah's elders and men gather to hear the book of the covenant, and its cities are cleansed of high places and idolatrous priests from Geba to Beersheba. The LORD nonetheless declares he will remove Judah from his sight because of Manasseh's provocation. Its land is later put under tribute to Pharaoh Necoh, and its kings Jehoahaz and Jehoiakim do evil.

l: Jerusalem, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 23
s: Jerusalem is where the king reads the covenant to the people, where idolatrous vessels, the Asherah, and altars are removed, and where the great Passover is kept in Josiah's eighteenth year. The LORD says he will cast off this city he chose, and the house where he said his name would be. Josiah's body is brought back there for burial, and Jehoahaz and Jehoiakim reign there.

l: Bethel, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 23
s: Josiah carries the ashes of the burned idolatrous vessels to Bethel. There he breaks down and burns the altar and high place made by Jeroboam son of Nebat, and burns bones from the tombs on the altar to defile it, fulfilling the word of the man of God. He leaves the tomb of that man of God undisturbed.

l: Passover, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 23
s: Josiah commands all the people to keep the Passover to the LORD as written in the book of the covenant. It is said that no such Passover had been kept since the days of the judges or in any days of the kings of Israel or Judah. It was kept in Jerusalem in Josiah's eighteenth year.

l: Pharaoh Necoh, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 23
s: Pharaoh Necoh, king of Egypt, goes up against the king of Assyria at the Euphrates and kills Josiah at Megiddo. He binds Jehoahaz at Riblah, takes him to Egypt, and imposes a tribute of one hundred talents of silver and a talent of gold. He makes Eliakim king as Jehoiakim, changing his name.

l: Jehoahaz, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 23
s: Jehoahaz, son of Josiah and Hamutal, is made king by the people of the land at age twenty-three and reigns three months. He does evil in the LORD's sight, is put in bonds by Pharaoh Necoh at Riblah, and is taken to Egypt, where he dies.

l: Jehoiakim, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 23
s: Jehoiakim, formerly Eliakim and son of Josiah and Zebidah, is made king by Pharaoh Necoh, who changes his name. He is twenty-five when he begins to reign and rules eleven years in Jerusalem. He taxes the people of the land to pay Pharaoh's tribute and does evil in the LORD's sight.

l: covenant, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 23
s: Standing by the pillar, Josiah makes a covenant before the LORD to walk after him and keep his commandments, testimonies, and statutes with all his heart and soul, confirming the words written in the book. All the people agree to the covenant.

l: Josiah's religious reforms, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 23
s: Josiah removes the vessels for Baal, the Asherah, and the army of the sky from the LORD's temple, removes idolatrous priests, and breaks down shrine prostitutes' houses, high places, and altars. He defiles Topheth and the high places Solomon built, destroys the Bethel altar, and extends the purge to Samaria's cities. He also removes mediums, wizards, teraphim, and idols, yet the LORD's wrath against Judah is not turned.

l: The Second Book of Kings, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 24
s: Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon came up against Judah, and Jehoiakim served him three years before rebelling, after which the LORD sent bands of Chaldeans, Syrians, Moabites and Ammonites against Judah because of Manasseh's sins and innocent bloodshed. Jehoiakim died and his son Jehoiachin, eighteen years old, reigned three months in Jerusalem and did evil. Babylon's servants besieged Jerusalem, and Jehoiachin surrendered with his mother, servants, princes and officers; Nebuchadnezzar took the temple and royal treasures, cut up Solomon's gold vessels, and deported the leading people, mighty men and craftsmen to Babylon, leaving only the poorest. Nebuchadnezzar made Mattaniah, Jehoiachin's father's brother, king and renamed him Zedekiah, who was twenty-one, reigned eleven years, did evil, and rebelled against the king of Babylon.

l: Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 24
s: Nebuchadnezzar came up against Judah, and Jehoiakim served him three years before rebelling. His servants besieged Jerusalem, and he captured Jehoiachin in the eighth year of his reign, carried off the temple and royal treasures, cut up Solomon's gold vessels, and deported the leading people to Babylon. He then made Mattaniah king in Jehoiachin's place and renamed him Zedekiah.

l: Jehoiakim, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 24
s: Jehoiakim served Nebuchadnezzar for three years and then rebelled against him. The LORD sent raiding bands against Judah in his time, and he died and was succeeded by his son Jehoiachin. His other acts are said to be in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Judah, and Zedekiah is later said to have done evil like all that he did.

l: Jehoiachin king of Judah, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 24
s: Jehoiachin became king at eighteen and reigned three months in Jerusalem; his mother was Nehushta daughter of Elnathan, and he did evil as his father had. He went out to the king of Babylon with his mother, servants, princes and officers and was captured, then carried to Babylon with his wives and officers.

l: Zedekiah, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 24
s: Zedekiah, formerly named Mattaniah and uncle of Jehoiachin, was made king by the king of Babylon, who changed his name. He was twenty-one when he began to reign, reigned eleven years in Jerusalem, and his mother was Hamutal daughter of Jeremiah of Libnah. He did evil like Jehoiakim and rebelled against the king of Babylon.

l: LORD, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 24
s: The LORD sent bands of Chaldeans, Syrians, Moabites and Ammonites against Judah, as he had spoken by his prophets. This was to remove Judah from his sight for Manasseh's sins and innocent blood, which he would not pardon. The text also says Babylon's removal of the temple treasures fulfilled what the LORD had said, and that his anger led to Judah and Jerusalem being cast out from his presence.

l: Judah, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 24
s: Judah was attacked by raiding bands sent by the LORD and removed from his sight because of Manasseh's sins and innocent blood. It was subjected to Babylon, lost its king Jehoiachin and its leading people to captivity, and was left with only the poorest. Its new king Zedekiah did evil and rebelled against Babylon.

l: Jerusalem, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 24
s: Jerusalem had been filled with innocent blood by Manasseh. It was besieged by Nebuchadnezzar's servants, and its king, treasures, princes, mighty men and craftsmen were taken to Babylon, leaving only the poorest people. Jehoiachin and Zedekiah both reigned there.

l: Babylon, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 24
s: Babylon, under Nebuchadnezzar, held all that had belonged to the king of Egypt from the brook of Egypt to the Euphrates, so Egypt's king no longer left his land. It became the destination of Jehoiachin, the royal household, and the deported people of Jerusalem, and its king installed Zedekiah, who later rebelled against him.

l: captives of Jerusalem (carried by Nebuchadnezzar), The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 24
s: Nebuchadnezzar carried away all Jerusalem, including the princes, ten thousand captives, mighty men of valor, craftsmen and smiths, with only the poorest left. The text also gives seven thousand men of might and one thousand craftsmen and smiths, all strong and fit for war, brought captive to Babylon. Jehoiachin, the king's mother, wives, officers and chief men were among them.

l: Babylonian exile/deportation of Judah, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 24
s: In the eighth year of Nebuchadnezzar's reign, after Jehoiachin surrendered, the king of Babylon took the treasures of the temple and palace and deported the king, his household, officials, mighty men and craftsmen from Jerusalem to Babylon. Only the poorest people remained, and the text frames this as the LORD's doing, as he had said.

l: siege of Jerusalem, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 24
s: Nebuchadnezzar's servants came up and besieged Jerusalem, and Nebuchadnezzar himself arrived while they were besieging it. It ended when Jehoiachin went out to the king of Babylon with his mother, servants, princes and officers and was captured.

l: The Second Book of Kings, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 25
s: Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon besieges Jerusalem until famine breaks the city in King Zedekiah's eleventh year; Zedekiah flees, is captured by the Chaldeans, watches his sons killed, is blinded, and is taken to Babylon. Nebuzaradan, captain of the guard, burns the LORD's house, the king's house and the city's houses, breaks down the walls, carries off the people and the bronze of the temple, and sends the chief officials to be executed at Riblah. Gedaliah is made governor over those left in Judah but is killed by Ishmael the son of Nethaniah, and the people flee to Egypt in fear of the Chaldeans.
