The chapter ends with Evilmerodach king of Babylon releasing Jehoiachin king of Judah from prison in the thirty-seventh year of his captivity and giving him a place of honor and a daily allowance for life.

l: Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 25
s: In his ninth year Nebuchadnezzar came with all his army against Jerusalem, encamped, and built forts around it. In his nineteenth year his captain Nebuzaradan came to Jerusalem and destroyed it, and Nebuchadnezzar had left Gedaliah as governor over the people remaining in Judah.

l: Jerusalem, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 25
s: Jerusalem was besieged until Zedekiah's eleventh year, when famine was severe and a breach was made in the city. Its walls were broken down and its houses burned, and the rest of its people were carried away captive, leaving only some of the poorest to work the vineyards and fields.

l: Zedekiah, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 25
s: Zedekiah fled by night by the way of the Arabah when the city was breached, but the Chaldean army overtook him in the plains of Jericho and his army scattered. He was taken to the king of Babylon at Riblah, where his sons were killed before his eyes, his eyes were put out, and he was bound in fetters and carried to Babylon.

l: Chaldeans, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 25
s: The Chaldeans surrounded the city, pursued and captured Zedekiah, and under Nebuzaradan broke down Jerusalem's walls and broke up the bronze of the LORD's house to carry it to Babylon. Some Chaldeans were with Gedaliah at Mizpah and were killed with him, and the people later fled to Egypt in fear of them.

l: Babylon, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 25
s: Babylon is where Zedekiah was carried in fetters and where the bronze of the LORD's house was taken. It is also where Jehoiachin was held and later honored by its king, who set his throne above the thrones of the kings with him there.

l: siege of Jerusalem, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 25
s: The siege began on the tenth day of the tenth month of Nebuchadnezzar's ninth year, with the Babylonians building forts around the city. It lasted until Zedekiah's eleventh year, when famine left no bread for the people and a breach was made in the city.

l: Nebuzaradan, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 25
s: Nebuzaradan, captain of the guard and servant of the king of Babylon, came to Jerusalem on the seventh day of the fifth month and burned the LORD's house, the king's house and the great houses. He carried away the remaining people, left some of the poorest, took the temple's bronze, gold and silver, and brought Seraiah, Zephaniah and other officials to the king at Riblah.

l: LORD's house, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 25
s: The LORD's house was burned by Nebuzaradan. The Chaldeans broke up its bronze pillars, bases and bronze sea and carried the bronze to Babylon, along with its pots, shovels, snuffers, spoons, fire pans, basins and gold and silver vessels. The bronze of Solomon's two pillars, the sea and the bases was not weighed, and the pillars are described as eighteen cubits high with three-cubit capitals.

l: Judah, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 25
s: Judah was carried away captive out of its land, and the king of Babylon put to death its leading officials at Riblah. Those left in the land were placed under Gedaliah, and after his murder the people, small and great, and the captains went to Egypt.

l: Gedaliah, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 25
s: Gedaliah, son of Ahikam and grandson of Shaphan, was made governor over the people left in Judah by Nebuchadnezzar. At Mizpah he swore to the captains and their men that they need not fear the Chaldeans and should dwell in the land and serve Babylon, but in the seventh month Ishmael struck him dead along with the Jews and Chaldeans with him.

l: Ishmael the son of Nethaniah, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 25
s: Ishmael, son of Nethaniah and of the royal offspring, was among the captains who came to Gedaliah at Mizpah. In the seventh month he came with ten men and killed Gedaliah, along with the Jews and Chaldeans who were with him.

l: Jehoiachin king of Judah, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 25
s: In the thirty-seventh year of his captivity, on the twenty-seventh day of the twelfth month, Jehoiachin was released from prison by Evilmerodach. He was spoken to kindly, given his prison garments changed, and ate bread before the king continually, receiving a daily allowance for all his life.

l: Evilmerodach king of Babylon, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 25
s: In the year he began to reign, Evilmerodach released Jehoiachin king of Judah from prison. He spoke kindly to him, set his throne above those of the kings with him in Babylon, and gave him a continual daily allowance for life.

l: Babylonian exile/deportation of Judah, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 25
s: Nebuzaradan carried away the rest of the people left in the city and those who had deserted to Babylon, leaving only some of the poorest of the land. The chapter says Judah was carried away captive out of his land, and it closes with Jehoiachin, in the thirty-seventh year of his captivity, being released from prison.

l: burning and destruction of Jerusalem, The Second Book of Kings, Chapter 25
s: On the seventh day of the fifth month of Nebuchadnezzar's nineteenth year, Nebuzaradan burned the LORD's house, the king's house, all the houses of Jerusalem and every great house. The Chaldean army broke down the walls around the city.

l: The Book of Job, The Book of Job, Chapter 1
s: Chapter 1 introduces Job, a blameless and upright man in the land of Uz who fears God, has seven sons and three daughters, and is the greatest of all the children of the east by virtue of his great wealth. Job regularly offers burnt offerings for his children in case they have sinned. When God's sons present themselves before the LORD, Satan comes among them and, after the LORD praises Job, argues that Job fears God only because he is blessed, and the LORD allows Satan to take all that Job has but not to touch Job himself. Four messengers then report in quick succession that the Sabeans took the oxen and donkeys, fire from the sky burned the sheep, the Chaldeans took the camels, and a great wind killed Job's children. Job tears his robe, shaves his head, and worships, saying the LORD gave and has taken away, and the text says he did not sin or charge God with wrongdoing.

l: Job, The Book of Job, Chapter 1
s: Job is introduced as a blameless, upright, God-fearing man in the land of Uz, with ten children and enormous wealth, who continually offers burnt offerings in case his sons have sinned. After losing his livestock, servants and all his children in a series of disasters, he tears his robe, shaves his head, falls to the ground and worships, blessing the LORD's name. The text states that in all this he did not sin or charge God with wrongdoing.

l: the LORD, The Book of Job, Chapter 1
s: The LORD receives God's sons and Satan, and points out Job as a servant like no one else on earth. He allows Satan to take all that Job has but forbids him to stretch out his hand against Job himself. Job acknowledges him as the one who gave and has taken away.

l: Satan, The Book of Job, Chapter 1
s: Satan comes among God's sons before the LORD, says he has been going back and forth on the earth, and challenges Job's piety, claiming Job fears God only because he has been protected and blessed. Given power over all that Job has, though not over Job himself, he goes out from the LORD's presence, and Job's possessions and children are then lost.

l: sons (Job's sons), The Book of Job, Chapter 1
s: Job's seven sons hold feasts in each one's house on his birthday and invite their three sisters to join them. Job sanctifies them and offers burnt offerings for them in case they have sinned. All of them die when a house collapses on them while they are eating and drinking wine in their oldest brother's house.

l: daughters (Job's daughters), The Book of Job, Chapter 1
s: Job's three daughters are invited by their brothers to eat and drink at the birthday feasts. They are with their brothers in the oldest brother's house when it falls, and they die with them.

l: messengers (Job's four messengers), The Book of Job, Chapter 1
s: Four messengers come to Job one after another, each speaking while the previous one is still talking. They report the Sabeans' raid on the oxen and donkeys, the fire of God burning the sheep and servants, the Chaldeans' seizure of the camels, and the death of Job's sons and daughters. Each says he alone has escaped to tell Job.

l: great wind (the wind that destroyed the house), The Book of Job, Chapter 1
s: A great wind comes from the wilderness and strikes the four corners of the oldest brother's house. The house falls on the young men and they die, as the fourth messenger reports to Job.

l: The Book of Job, The Book of Job, Chapter 2
s: On another day when God's sons present themselves before the LORD, Satan comes among them and the LORD points to Job as blameless and still faithful despite Satan's earlier incitement. Satan argues that a man will give everything for his own life and says Job will renounce God if his bone and flesh are touched. The LORD places Job in Satan's hand but forbids him to take Job's life, and Satan strikes Job with painful sores from foot to head. Job sits among ashes scraping himself with a potsherd, rejects his wife's urging to renounce God and die, and does not sin with his lips. His three friends, Eliphaz, Bildad and Zophar, come to comfort him, weep and tear their robes on seeing him, and sit silently with him on the ground for seven days and nights.

l: Job, The Book of Job, Chapter 2
s: Job is described by the LORD as blameless, upright, God-fearing and still maintaining his integrity. Struck with painful sores from head to foot, he sits among the ashes scraping himself with a potsherd. He rebukes his wife, asking whether people should receive good from God and not evil, and does not sin with his lips.

l: Satan, The Book of Job, Chapter 2
s: Satan comes among God's sons to present himself before the LORD, saying he has been going back and forth on the earth. He argues that Job will renounce God if his bone and flesh are touched. Given Job into his hand with his life spared, he strikes Job with painful sores.

l: the LORD, The Book of Job, Chapter 2
s: The LORD asks Satan where he has come from and holds up Job as blameless, upright and still maintaining his integrity. He says Satan incited him against Job without cause. He puts Job in Satan's hand but commands that Job's life be spared.

l: wife (Job's wife), The Book of Job, Chapter 2
s: Job's wife asks him whether he still maintains his integrity and tells him to renounce God and die. Job answers that she speaks like one of the foolish women.

l: Eliphaz the Temanite, The Book of Job, Chapter 2
s: Eliphaz the Temanite is one of Job's three friends who hear of his evil and come from his own place. He makes an appointment with the others to sympathize with and comfort Job, and joins in weeping, tearing his robe and sitting silently seven days and nights.

l: Bildad the Shuhite, The Book of Job, Chapter 2
s: Bildad the Shuhite is one of Job's three friends who hear of his troubles and come from his own place. He makes an appointment with the others to comfort Job, and joins in weeping, tearing his robe and sitting silently seven days and nights.

l: Zophar the Naamathite, The Book of Job, Chapter 2
s: Zophar the Naamathite is one of Job's three friends who hear of his troubles and come from his own place. He makes an appointment with the others to comfort Job, and joins in weeping, tearing his robe and sitting silently seven days and nights.

l: three friends (Job's friends), The Book of Job, Chapter 2
s: Job's three friends come separately from their own places by appointment to sympathize with and comfort him. They do not recognize him from a distance, weep aloud, tear their robes and sprinkle dust on their heads toward the sky. They sit with him on the ground seven days and nights without speaking, seeing that his grief is very great.

l: Job's suffering, The Book of Job, Chapter 2
s: Job's suffering begins when Satan, with the LORD's permission, strikes him with painful sores from the sole of his foot to his head. It is limited by the LORD's command to spare his life. It is made worse by his wife's urging to renounce God, and his grief is called very great by the friends who sit with him.

l: The Book of Job, The Book of Job, Chapter 3
s: In Chapter 3, Job breaks his silence and curses the day of his birth and the night of his conception, wishing them darkness, barrenness, and erasure from the calendar. He blames that night for not shutting the doors of his mother's womb or hiding trouble from his eyes. Job asks why he did not die at birth, imagining the rest he would have in death alongside kings, princes, the wicked, the weary, prisoners, and servants. He then asks why light and life are given to the miserable and bitter in soul who long for death, and to a man whose way is hidden and whom God has hedged in. He ends by describing his sighing, groaning, fear, and lack of rest, as trouble comes upon him.

l: Job, The Book of Job, Chapter 3
s: Job opens his mouth and curses the day of his birth, wishing it and the night of his conception had never been. He asks why he did not die at birth, imagining death as rest among kings, princes, and the weary. He describes himself as sighing and groaning, never at ease, and overtaken by the thing he feared, as trouble comes.

l: day of Job's birth, The Book of Job, Chapter 3
s: Job curses this day, asking that it perish and become darkness. He asks that God not seek it, that no light shine on it, and that a cloud, the shadow of death, and all that blackens the day terrify and claim it.

l: night of Job's conception, The Book of Job, Chapter 3
s: Job curses this night, asking that thick darkness seize it, that it not be counted among the days or months, and that it be barren with no joyful voice. He blames it for not shutting the doors of his mother's womb and not hiding trouble from his eyes.

l: death, The Book of Job, Chapter 3
s: Job pictures death as a place of quiet and rest, where he would lie with kings, counselors, and princes, like a hidden untimely birth. There the wicked cease from troubling, the weary rest, prisoners are at ease, the small and great are together, and the servant is free from his master. Job says the miserable long for it and dig for it more than for hidden treasures, rejoicing when they find the grave.

l: the miserable, The Book of Job, Chapter 3
s: Job asks why light is given to those in misery and life to the bitter in soul. They long for death, but it does not come, and they dig for it more than for hidden treasure and are glad when they find the grave.

l: trouble, The Book of Job, Chapter 3
s: Job says the night did not hide trouble from his eyes. He ends the chapter saying he has no ease, quiet, or rest, but trouble comes.

l: The Book of Job, The Book of Job, Chapter 4
s: Eliphaz the Temanite answers Job, asking whether Job will be grieved by his speaking and noting that Job has previously instructed and strengthened others but now faints when trouble touches him. Eliphaz asks whether Job's piety and integrity are not his confidence and hope, and argues from what he has seen that the innocent do not perish while those who plow iniquity and sow trouble reap the same. He says such people perish by the breath of God, likening them to lions whose teeth are broken and whose cubs are scattered. Eliphaz then recounts a night vision in which a spirit passed before his face and a voice spoke out of silence. The voice asks whether mortal man can be more just or pure than God, says God does not trust his servants and charges his angels with error, and concludes that those who dwell in houses of clay are destroyed and die without wisdom.

l: Eliphaz the Temanite, The Book of Job, Chapter 4
s: Eliphaz the Temanite answers Job, asking whether Job will be grieved if he speaks, and observes that Job has strengthened others but now faints under trouble. He argues that the innocent never perish and the wicked reap what they sow, then relates a secret night vision in which he heard a voice about the injustice of mortals before God.

l: Job (the addressee of Eliphaz), The Book of Job, Chapter 4
s: Job is addressed by Eliphaz as one who has instructed many and strengthened weak hands and feeble knees, but who now faints and is troubled when trouble touches him. Eliphaz asks whether Job's piety and the integrity of his ways are not his confidence and hope.

l: God, The Book of Job, Chapter 4
s: God is said by Eliphaz to destroy those who sow trouble by his breath and the blast of his anger. In the voice from the vision, God is described as more just and more pure than mortal man, as not trusting his servants, and as charging his angels with error.

l: spirit (seen by Eliphaz in a night vision), The Book of Job, Chapter 4
s: A spirit passed before Eliphaz's face, making the hair of his flesh stand up. It stood still with a form Eliphaz could not discern, and after silence a voice spoke.

l: those who plow iniquity and sow trouble, The Book of Job, Chapter 4
s: Eliphaz says that, according to what he has seen, those who plow iniquity and sow trouble reap the same. They perish by the breath of God and are consumed by the blast of his anger, like lions whose teeth are broken, who perish for lack of prey, and whose cubs are scattered.

l: mortal man, The Book of Job, Chapter 4
s: The voice in Eliphaz's vision asks whether mortal man can be more just than God or more pure than his Maker. Mortals are described as dwelling in houses of clay with foundations in the dust, crushed before the moth, destroyed between morning and evening, and dying without wisdom.

l: night vision, The Book of Job, Chapter 4
s: Eliphaz says a thing was secretly brought to him in thoughts from the visions of the night, when deep sleep falls on men. Fear and trembling made all his bones shake, a spirit passed before him, and a voice delivered a message about the justice of God and the frailty of man.

l: divine justice and retribution, The Book of Job, Chapter 4
s: Eliphaz claims that no innocent person has perished and that those who plow iniquity and sow trouble reap the same, perishing by God's breath and anger. The voice in his vision adds that no mortal is more just or pure than God, who even charges his angels with error.

l: The Book of Job, The Book of Job, Chapter 5
s: In Chapter 5 a speaker addresses a listener, asking whether any of the holy ones will answer him, and warns that resentment and jealousy kill the foolish and simple. He recounts seeing a foolish man take root and then cursing his dwelling, with the man's children crushed in the gate and his harvest eaten by the hungry. He says affliction does not spring from the ground, but man is born to trouble as sparks fly upward. The speaker says he would seek God and commit his cause to him, praising God for marvelous works, for giving rain, for lifting the lowly, for frustrating the crafty, and for saving the needy so the poor have hope. He closes by calling happy the man whom God corrects, promising the listener deliverance in famine, war, and trouble, peace with the animals, a secure tent, great offspring, and a full age, and says this has been researched and is true.

l: God, The Book of Job, Chapter 5
s: God is said to do great, unfathomable and countless marvelous things, giving rain on the earth and sending water on the fields. He sets the lowly on high, raises mourners to safety, frustrates the plans of the crafty, and saves the needy from the sword of their mouth and the hand of the mighty. He wounds and binds up, injures and makes whole, and the speaker says he would seek God and commit his cause to him.

l: the foolish man (the foolish), The Book of Job, Chapter 5
s: The foolish man is killed by resentment, and the simple by jealousy. The speaker saw him taking root but suddenly cursed his habitation. His children are far from safety and crushed in the gate with no deliverer, and the hungry eat his harvest, even taking it out of the thorns, while a snare gapes for his substance.
